query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing the surface of boride-based components to form a thin, continuous alumina (Al2O3) layer will improve their resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components (e.g., parts containing refractory borides) as currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment without any preformed protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled high‐temperature pre-oxidation treatment in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., heating in ambient air) to intentionally form a stable, dense alumina scale on the surface.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment at approximately 800 °C for about 1 hour in air to produce the oxide layer, with subsequent exposure to molten aluminum at typical plating temperatures (around 700–750 °C) for durations representative of service conditions (e.g., hundreds of hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formed alumina layer, which is known to have low diffusivity and high chemical stability at elevated temperatures, will serve as a diffusion barrier between the boride substrate and the molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 scale acts as an inert, protective barrier that slows down or prevents the infiltration and reaction of molten aluminum with the underlying boride phase. By hindering direct contact and interdiffusion, the oxide layer reduces the dissolution of boride constituents and mitigates corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the corrosion rate (e.g., lower weight loss and reduced surface degradation) when compared to untreated boride components, meaning that the pre-oxidized components will display improved stability and longevity during exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components that have not undergone the pre-oxidation treatment, which under molten aluminum conditions show higher degradation rates due to direct chemical attack and dissolution.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected to persist at plating temperatures up to about 750 °C provided the oxide scale remains continuous and intact. Mechanical damage to the scale or environments with additional fluxing species might compromise the protection.
generation.uncertainty: While the general protective nature of alumina in high-temperature environments is well established, the precise quantitative improvement (i.e., percentage reduction in corrosion rate) and long-term stability under dynamic cycling (thermal/mechanical stresses) in this specific molten-aluminum environment remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically fabricated boride-based component samples. One set is subjected to the pre-oxidation treatment (800 °C, 1 hour in air) to form the alumina scale, while the other set is left untreated. Both sets are then immersed in molten aluminum at ~720 °C for an extended period (e.g., 500 hours) under controlled conditions. After exposure, evaluate changes using weight loss measurements, microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS) to examine scale continuity and phase transformations, and XRD to detect any corrosive products.
measurements: SEM/EDS analysis of surface morphology (integrity of the alumina layer and presence of corrosion attack)
XRD phase analysis of surface and near-surface regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar weight losses, surface degradation, and phase changes compared to untreated samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Therefore, in order to investigate the high-temperature protective capabilities of EHEA coatings, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 co-doping with Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding in this paper. After their preparation, the microstructure and high-temperature thermal stability of the coatings were characterized, and the hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% (wt.%) NaCl mixed molten salt was investigated, which provided data support for an evaluation of the potential applications of high-entropy alloy coatings in harsh service environments such as steam pipelines and the hot-end components of gas turbines.

AbstractThe corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5, which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions.Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys
